paras: The threatened lynching of Bill Miles was a reported plan in August 1888 by friends of Capt. Nat Kinney, chief of the Bald Knobbers, to lynch Miles, who had shot and killed Kinney in Taney County, Missouri. No attack on Miles was reported; he was released on bond within days and indicted for first-degree murder in October. Papers across the country carried the story because of Kinney's fame as the Bald Knobber founder, warning of "a serious outbreak" if Miles was not hanged.

Kinney was described as the founder and chief of the Bald Knobbers, a band that a Springfield dispatch said had ruled the hills of Christian County from 1884 to 1887. According to an Ozark dispatch, his killing grew out of the "Berry-Taylor feud," which had kept Forsyth expecting bloodshed for two months. Kinney had been appointed by the court as receiver of the hardware store of a man named Berry, an "extreme anti-Knobber," and a later dispatch said Berry had recently had his wife arrested for adultery.

The Ozark dispatch said Kinney died at Forsyth on the morning of August 20 after a quarrel with William Miles in a store, in which Miles fired five shots before Kinney could level his pistol. A second Ozark dispatch, dated August 24 and citing a courier from Forsyth, called the killing a conspiracy in which the Berry party chose Miles to provoke a quarrel and shoot Kinney, three times in Berry's store and twice more on the floor.

The same courier reported that the "remnants of the old band of Bald Knobbers" were organizing to lynch Miles, and that the jail was guarded by a posse the sheriff had specially sworn in. A Springfield dispatch printed by the Forrest City Times told a different story, placing the shooting late at night at Ozark, Christian County, and saying Miles escaped, "pursued by an angry mob of fifty of Kinney's warmest supporters." It added that bloodhounds had been sent for from Harrison, Arkansas.

A Springfield dispatch of August 24 said Miles had waived examination and been released on bond, and that the inquest had shown the killing to be premeditated and prearranged. It added that if the Bald Knobbers were not certain Miles would be sentenced to hang, "he would undoubtedly have been lynched before this." On October 11 a Springfield dispatch reported that the Taney County grand jury had indicted Miles, printed as "Wm. Mills," for first-degree murder and J. S. D. Berry as an accessory before the fact, and that both were jailed without bail.

In November the Mountain Echo of Yellville, Arkansas, reported that Berry and Miles had been released on bonds of $8,000 each after a hearing before Judge Hubbard at Ozark, and that a change of venue was likely. No report of a trial or its outcome appears in the coverage.

White papers learned of the threat mainly through the Springfield wire item, which the Washington Critic ran on August 24 as "Bill Miles Released." The next day the St. Paul Daily Globe printed it as "An Eye for an Eye," with a deck promising that Kinney's friends would "See to It That His Slayer Swings." The Wilmington Daily Republican and the Beatrice Daily Express also ran it on August 25, and the Middleburgh Post in Pennsylvania reprinted it on August 30 as "Bound to Hang Him."

The Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian headed the courier's report "In Danger of Being Hanged" and "Capt. Kinney's Friends Determined to Avenge His Death." The Forrest City Times called Kinney's followers "the boldest band of outlaws that ever disgraced the Southwest" yet predicted that his death "will not go unavenged." None of the reports gave the race of Miles, Kinney or Berry.

Accounts differed on where Kinney was killed: most placed it at Forsyth in Taney County, while a wire brief and the Forrest City Times placed it at Ozark in Christian County. The Forsyth version agrees with the later indictment by the Taney County grand jury. Reports also disagreed on Miles's situation during the threats, describing him as held in a guarded jail, free on bond of $5,000 or $4,000, or a fugitive chased by a mob.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Bill Miles
bases: Friends of the slain Nat Kinney and 'remnants of the old band of Bald Knobbers' were reported organizing to lynch Bill Miles, and one account had a mob of fifty pursuing him, but no attack on him was reported (A3, A5, A10).
Miles was threatened and, in one account, pursued by a mob of fifty seeking revenge for Kinney, but no report has him killed or harmed; he was released on bond and later indicted (A3, A10, A5, A11).

Separate Ozark and Springfield dispatches agree that Kinney's Bald Knobber friends meant to lynch Miles (A3, A5, A10), though they disagree on the place of the killing and on whether Miles was jailed, bailed or at large (A4, A5, A10).

accounts.label: Ozark dispatch (Aug. 21)
accounts.gist: Kinney died at Forsyth after a quarrel with Miles in a store; Kinney drew first but Miles fired five shots before he could aim.

accounts.label: Forsyth courier via Ozark (Aug. 24)
accounts.gist: The killing was a conspiracy of the Berry party, with Miles chosen to provoke Kinney and shoot him; Bald Knobber remnants were organizing to lynch Miles and the jail was under a sworn guard.

accounts.label: Springfield wire (Aug. 24)
accounts.gist: Miles waived examination and was released on bond; the inquest found premeditation; he would already have been lynched if the Bald Knobbers did not expect him to hang.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch (Forrest City Times)
accounts.gist: The men fought late at night at Ozark, Christian County, and fired almost together; Miles escaped, chased by a mob of fifty, and bloodhounds were sent for.

framing.detail: The Yankton paper headlined the courier's report 'In Danger of Being Hanged' with 'Capt. Kinney's Friends Determined to Avenge His Death.'
The St. Paul Globe's 'An Eye for an Eye' and the Middleburgh Post's 'Bound to Hang Him' presented a hanging sentence as the alternative to a lynching and an 'outbreak.'
The Forrest City Times called Kinney's band the boldest outlaws 'that ever disgraced the Southwest' while predicting his death would 'not go unavenged.'
The Washington Critic, Wilmington Daily Republican and Beatrice Daily Express ran the Springfield bond report nearly verbatim.
